He asks the Government to assume that when he advises the Government he does not mean what he says; indeed, does not know what he is talking about.

I have listened this
afternoon with a good deal of interest to the remarks of the member for Welland (Mr. German), as I always do, and also to what the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) has said. Really I do not know what the Solicitor General is driving at.
The member for Welland.

Then my hon. friend's aim was very poor. He failed both to reach his mark and to make it clear what he was aiming at. Every man in the committee is entitled to have views of his own, and he ought not to be kicked around too badly if he expresses them. Anyway, I am going to take the responsibility of giving some of my views on this question. First, I may say that I cannot agree with the Government; neither can I agree with the member for Welland. I do not believe that any member of Parliament ought to be asked to vote for a proposal which he thinks is unsound, simply because the juggernaut is going and public opinion is such

that it ought not to be withstood. My opinion has always been that if a man has opinions of his own, he had better assert them and try afterwards to convince the public that he is right. If he is not right, then he cau let the public do what they have a mind to do about it. That may be a very independent attitude, but I have alwaj s taken to at v'ew.
I do not believe in public ownership cf any kind. I do object to the Government going as far as they are going in respect to the proposed ownership of the Canadian Northern railway system. The Ministei of Finance stated that it was the intention to appoint a commission that should be subject to Parliament, not to the Government. Well, if the Government can do that, it is a wonderful step in the right direction. But no man who has lived in the Maritime Provinces all his life as I have done can honestly say that he is in favour of the public ownership of railways. I know that in Ontario there is a fetisih in respect of public ownership; men are worshipping the public ownership of everything. But it will not be many years before they come back to sound business principles. We had an illustration of that in the House the other evening. In Ontario they have had public ownership-of utilities in the way of electrical energy- the greatest administration of electrical energy which the world has known. There is no doubt that the Hydro-Electric Commission of Ontario has done wonderful work. But they are commencing to get up against the wall. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) was compelled to call upon his supporters to vote for an amendment to the general Railway Act of Canada absolutely to put out of existence a competitor to the Hydro-Electric because it stood in the way of this juggernaut. You would not find a better illustration in the records of Canada, from Confederation down to the present time, of the failure of public ownership.

That is hardly a fair
statement. The reason why the Conservatives voted as they did on that point was stated in the committee when that company was getting its rights from this Government. It was that the rights of the municipality in certain streets should be protected. Sir Edmund Osier asked to have this amendment put in, and he was told by the minister and by the lawyer who was putting the matter through, that it was put in.

I am not going to go into the details of that. I simply bring it up as an illustration to show that when public ownership starts out to usurp the proper functions of business men, those who have charge always come to the end of their tether; they always come to the time when they cannot carry on things as a business proposition, and then they have to resort to power of some kind in order to work out their scheme, exactly as the HydroElectric did in the case in question.
There was another point made by my hon. friend which struck me very strongly and that was that, in his judgment, there ought not to be arbitration under present conditions. He illustrated the fact that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Eogers) commenced his public career about the same time as the Canadian Northern Railway company began their career in Manitoba as railway builders. He naturally would argue from that, that the people of Manitoba should have gone on with public ownership and not have public utilities handed over to the Canadian Northern or Mackenzie, Mann and Company. He referred to the devious ways of Mackenzie, Mann and Company and the Minister of Public Works during some years that followed in Manitoba politics, and I think he naturally would have drawn the conclusion that all the troubles were because in Manitoba they had not adhered to the principle of public ownership in railways. The path trod by these firms in Manitoba was a "Great White Way" in comparison with the path trod by an hon. gentleman in Manitoba over the question of public telephones. If in the political history of Canada there is a paragraph or chapter that absolutely condemns public ownership of any public utility in this country, it is the story of the administration of the telephone system in Manitoba during the last seven or eight years. From the very inception of the purchase of the Bell Telephone system in Manitoba down to about three years ago, the path has been one which I would not want to follow, which I do not believe any hon. gentleman in this House would want to follow, and which, in so far as any one instance will condemn a system, must condemn public ownership of public utilities in Canada. If the minister could operate the Canadian Northern Railway system entirely free from political interference, he might get along fairly well, but certainly not as well as private enterprise would get along. He cannot, however, do that; he cannot run a railway in Canada of the magnitude of the Canadian Northern and keep political influence out of it. We have had an experience of that in the Maritime Provinces. I believe the present Minister of Railways started out to run the Intercolonial for a year or two fairly divorced from politics, but two years had not passed before you could not hire a man to bhovel gravel for two days at a time unless he went to the man who controlled the patronage in the constituency, and that has been the case ever since. It is idle to speak about hiring a man on the Intercolonial who is not recommended by the man who controls the patronage, and the minister knows that. The minister knows it would be as impossible for him to hire twenty-five men who were not recommended by the man who controls the patronage in their constituency las it would be for him to fly.
The trouble nowadays is to get men, no matter who recommends them.
The minister knows he has to have the recommendation of the patronage committee.
That is not true.
My hon. friend knows it is true.
It is not true.

I tell the minister it is true. The minister may think it is not true; he may think he is not administering the railway in that fashion, but if he asks his general manager what he can do in the face of the patronage committees, he will find that the general manager is absolutely powerless. I do not believe the minister can run the Canadian Northern, which is about ten times the magnitude of the Intercolonial, as a Government road and keep patronage out of it.
The Government do not intend to do so.

I do not think they do, because I find in the last clause of the resolution these words:
That the necessary qualification shares for directors may be transferred to or allowed to remain in their names by the Minister of Finance on such conditions as he may determine.
That simply means that the Minister of Finance or the Government appoint the directors under such conditions as they may determine. They put enough stock in a director's hands to qualify him, but he is

simply a creature of the Government; he sits on the hoard as a member of the political machine, and'the road will be run as the greatest political machine Canada has ever known. Think of the Minister of Railways running hotels, telegraphs, telephones, townsites, express-
Steamboats.
Would not that make us practically owners of the road, which is what my hon. friend objects to?

We are that now. The moment we took over 40 per cent of the stock of the Canadian Northern in 1914, *we became, not legally, but as a matter of practical business, the owners of the road and became bound to see the thing through no matter what happened.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
is making a very fair argument, and I do not like to interrupt him. As I understand it, he has suggested that we should make an advance of $20,000,000 and that we take a certain amount of stock as secur-

ity. W'hat would my hon. friend do this time next year, when the same question would arise again, and $20,000,000 more be needed to pay the interest on the underlying securities?
I do not know. I should be in the same position as my hon. friend was in two years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think we had better deal with it now.

We hope the war will be over this time next year. That is a wish that I am sure every hon. member of this House and every one in this country sincerely joins in, and when the war is over, things will be clear that are now dark. We can then grapple with the whole railway situation, ascertaining exactly what our financial liabilities and the prospects for the future are. But, as it is, we are here embarking the country on a scheme involving an expenditure of $140,000,000 or $150,000,000, and under a management which cannot possibly be economical or businesslike from any standpoint. I was reading this afternoon the minority report of Mr. Smith, and was very much impressed with two statements that I read. They so thoroughly coincided with my own views that I feel like placing them on Hansard. The first is found on page 102:
Compared with the total outlay involved in producing railroads by the Government for itself, as, for instance, the case of the Intercolonial or the Transcontinental, from three to six times that amount have been used to realize equal results. This shows distinctly the value of enlisting and retaining private enterprise.
If this statement be true, that the governments of this country from Confederation down to the present time have spent in building Government roads six times as much as the Canadian Northern has spent-and he was dealing directly with that company-it is an amazing statement. It so attracted my attention that I read it two or three times. I do not mean to say that the Canadian Northern lines are in as good a state physically as the Government lines. Mr. Smith, after discussing what government ownership would mean, the extra cost of construction, operation and management -and he certainly puts up a pretty strong argument against government ownership- concludes with these words:
Upon these fundamental truths, I base my firm conviction that the brightest outlook for the future of your great Dominion can be assured through the extension of private railroad enterprises. The hope of honour and the reward of public approval must he open to
human kind to get the best results from human endeavour.
I tell you, Mr. Chairman, that if you take away from the Canadian Northern enterprise the hope of honour and reward, the ambition of the human being, you will absolutely divest it of everything that has made it the great enterprise it is to-day, and there is no disguising the fact that it is a great enterprise. I do not know whether money has been taken out of the road or not. I am something like my hon. friend from Welland in that respect I do not believe that they have handled $400,000,000 without using a little on the side for their own purposes, although I have no evidence to that effect. I should like, however, to see a statement in writing, not to say an affidavit, that such is not the case. There is no use shutting our eyes to the fact that Mackenzie and Mann have worked up a wonderful railway organization in Canada. Their financing has been a marvel; I do not know how they have done it. They have built up an organization of very bright men.

They have got money
from the Government.

The Government might hand over $400,000,000 to my hon. friend or myself, 'but I do not think either of us would get the same results with it that Mackenzie and Mann have. I give them credit for that. I think they are wizards of finance. I do not think the public have given them sufficient credit for the manner in which they have handled that end of the business. Then there is a wonderful personal element Tunning through their whole system. I know a number of their men, and perhaps I may be pardoned for mentioning two who, outside the principals, I regard as the greatest among them-Mr. Hanna and Mr. Moore. These gentlemen have impressed their personality^and many others besides them-on the whole organization from top to bottom. The Government may take over this system and say, "We are going to keep Mackenzie and Mann and some of their organization," but they will not be able to do it. Once the present officials realize that political power is interfering with their management, it will not be six months 'before they, if not Mackenzie and Mann themselves, will say, "I won't have a member of Parliament dismissing or appointing a man through his political influence." It would not be six months before the whole present organization would be disbanded and gone. I do not see any necessity for doing away with the men who

are absolutely necessary to keep this enterprise going. I do not see any necessity lor the Government taking over control of the road. I believe the present organization can run the road better than the Government. I believe that sufficient money should be put up to pay off the company's indebtedness, and as much of the stock should be taken over as is available, for extra security-not that I think the stock is worth anything. I believe that five-sixths of the stock would be available. With five-sixths of the stock in their hands there would be no question as to the Government having control over the road, and if Mackenzie and Mann were not handling things properly, the Government would have it in their power to interfere at any time. That, of course, involves the next question, whether or not the Government should go on and buy out whatever the equity of Mackenzie and Mann may be.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

When the committee adjourned at six o'clock I wias giving some reasons why I was opposed to public ownership of railways in particular, and of public utilities in general. I was pointing out that in my opinion the Government should put up whatever money was absolutely necessary to tide over the Canadian Northern for a year, and see what the future would have in store for us. I was pointing out, also, that in my judgment the personal element in the present Canadian Northern organization means a great deal. I still believe they can manage the affairs of the railway, 'both from the operating standpoint and from the financial standpoint, very much better than the Government of Canada oo-uld. I find, in looking over the statement laid upon the Table, as to the liabilities that are maturing within the next year, that $3,000,000 off equipment notes are maturing; about $10,000,000 of different bonds are maturing in London, and there are other large amounts off bonds payable on demand outstanding in Canada. There are also $10,000,000 of demand securities for liabilities in London. Thus $35,000,000 to $40,000,000 of securities or liabilities mature within the next year, or on demand. The moment the Government of Canada takes over the stock of this road and makes it a Government-owned and Government-controlled proposition, depend

upon it every dollar of that money will have to be paid. It is very simple. The price cf money is going up every day, and a man who has funds invested at four and a half or five per cent, with the Government of Canada behind it, will say; " I want the money," and the Government of Canada will have to raise it, because reinvestment can be made at a much better rate of interest. My contention is that if the Canadian Northern were still running this enterprise they could go to those people 'and say: "we cannot give you your money; there is no use talking about it, we have not the money, and we cannot get it; we will pay your interest, but you must renew the principal." I believe they could renew it on a basis that would mean millions of dollars over and above what could be done by the Government if it were taken over. If the Government takes the railway over it will have to pay every dollar in full at maturity, and will have to go to the markets of the world and borrow this money. Speaking offhand, I cannot see how we are going to get along on less than $100,000,000 of actual money, which this country must produce next year if we take over the road, to carry out the proposals as set forth in this resolution, while, as I say, I believe the Canadian Northern organization could finance it on one-third of that amount. They do like the rest of us when we get hard up and cannot pay our debts in full. Of course, I know this does not apply to the Minister of Finance, because he has lots of money. When I say "the rest of us" I mean some of my friends around me.
Bailiff-proof.

more than the liabilities -or worth perhaps *as much; but they will be able to show an earning capacity which you are taking away from them, and you are taking away that earning capacity just at the time when it becomes a real earning capacity-because up to the last few years it has been problematical, but now it is a real earning capacity-and you are going to say to an arbitration : you will have to take all these matters into consideration. We all know how these things go. I know from my little experience with arbitrations of right of way and other things in connection with railways, all these matters must be taken into consideration; and the result will he that we will pay to Mackenzie and Mann $10,000,000 or $20,000,000 or $30,000,000, which we ought not to pay and which we have no license to pay to them at the present time. But, on the other hand, if they, through their energy and ability, have worked up an organization which has a money-earning capacity, then let them work it out. Why take it away from them? Why pay them money which they (have not earned? Rather leave it in their hands and let them work it out, and if there is any money in it let them make it. I think, myself, that if you allowed this road to go on for four or five years more it would be iself-sustaining. I realize that next year we iwill probably have to put up more money, and, perhaps, the year after. But we are in it. I think it was ian improvident bargain three years ago. When the proposal to guarantee $45,000,000 was up I was opposed to it, and, while I have net looked up my remarks, I have a very good recollection of the attitude I took. I was opposed to granting the $45,000,000. Then, in .addition to that, you have granted them $15,000,000, making $60,000,000, and now you are proposing to put up $100,000,000 next year. I say that is not good financing .under present conditions; it is not good 'business for Canada. The proper business for Canada .at this time is to put u.p just as little money as she can get along with and leave this road in the 'hands of the men who have made it a fairly successful enterprise up to the present time, taking, of course, all the security which they can give you, taking the stock, enough of it to put it beyond question that you have a majority and have control. In fact, I would take practically all the stock. I would hold 'it as a trustee and let these people go on and see if they cannot work out theiT own salvation. It will not become any worse in -a year, because if you control the 
expenditure of money which you put up it will not be wasted, and the .property will increase its earning capacity. You will not have to spend the $100,000,000 that we are going to spend next year, and if you (have to take the road over a year from now, or two years from now, you will have saved probably $50,000,000 or $75,000,000.
That brings me to the last .point I wish to discuss, that is, the method of arriving at the amount of compensation, if compensation is rto be paid. I entirely .agree with my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) in the statement he made this afternoon. I do not believe in handing this over to an arbitration board. I believe the arbitration would go at the matter in a sentimental way, in a manner which a judge of the Exchequer Court would not. If we have to arbitrate or to pay Mackenzie and . Mann for their equity, surely the determination of the amount to be paid them should be put in the hands of a man who will apply all the technical rules and knowledge which ought to be applied in arriving at the real value of this enterprise. We have all had experience with arbitrations. I do not believe there is a lawyer in this House who, if he is honest, will not tell you that he has all his lifetime advised clients not to arbitrate.
I have laid it down almost as a settled rule in my practice, invariably to advise clients not to arbitrate, because arbitrators, appointed as -you appoint them here, will always give and take. One party will build up an unreasonable contention. I will venture to say that Mackenzie and Mann will claim before this board that they are entitled to $100,000,000, and no doubt the Government arbitrator will say: You are entitled to nothing. Then they will go on and argue and argue, and finally divide the difference. That is what happens in most arbitrations, and the result will be that Mackenzie and Mann will get three times what they are entitled to. Whereas if this is given over to the Exchequer Court you will at least have it decided on well-known principles which should govern the assessment of compensation in matters of this kind. So, Sir, for these reasons, I am very much opposed to the proposals contained in this resolution, and I hope the Government, even at this late date, will see their way clear to reconsider the matter and to put up as little money as they can to tide this road over for a year, or possibly two years, in the hope that the war will end-and surely it will end in that time. If, at that time, you had only the Canadian Northern

to deal with, there would not he such a strong argument for delay; but you have still the great railway problem of Canada, staring you in the face. If you take over the Canadian Northern, have you settled the railway question? No, we have the Grand Trunk Pacific, we have the National Transcontinental and we have the Intercolonial.
And the branch lines.

We have the branch lines -branch lines all over Canada. Why, if the government of this country talk about taking over the Canadian Northern because they cannot run, how in the world are they going to avoid taking over branch lines all over the country which cannot run for lack of finances? The Minister of Marine (Mr. Hazen) knows that in his own constituency there is a branch line which practically is being closed down because they cannot get finances to run it. I realize that it is a small enterprise compared with the Canadian Northern, but it is as important to the people in that constituency as the Canadian Northern is to the people in. any other part of Canada. How will the Government justify taking over the Canadian Northern and leaving other systems in Canada, small though they may be, that are unable to run because of lack of funds? Every branch line of the Intercolonial-and I refer to the Intercolonial because I presume there are very few branch lines elsewhere that do not belong to the big systems-has just as much right to come to the Finance Minister and say: We cannot go on without financial assistance, and to claim financial assistance, as the Canadian Northern. And my hon. friend is establishing a principle which he cannot get away from. He is establishing a principle which must be followed out in every portion of Canada.
So, Sir, for these reasons, I can only say that I hope the Government will stop to consider and see if they cannot withdraw from the position they have taken; put up just the least possible amount of money in order to keep this enterprise going for a year or two; and then you will have the whole railway situation-or whatever government may be here at the time, because I think it is very doubtful if my hon. friend will be the gentleman who will have to work it out, but somebody will.
For this and other reasons.

The Government will
have the whole problem of the railways
of Canada to face at that time, and it is much better to face these questions after the war is over, when we know what our liabilities are, how much money we are going to raise, and where we are going to raise it. We will start out with a knowledge of the actual condition of affairs, which is better than starting out now on an expenditure of $100,000,000 to $150,000,000 but I do not believe that the Finance Minister knows where he is going to look around and get the money.

What are the
maturities of the Canadian Northern within the next fifteen months that the Government would be obliged to extend, and what, in the judgment of the Finance Minister, is the least amount that should be advanced in the next fifteen months for equipment? I understood the hon. gentleman to say the net earnings could take eare of the interest account, providing it is not expended upon equipment, extensions and betterments.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The financial
position of the Canadian Northern is substantially this. Assuming net earnings of $11,000,000, the Canadian Northern have to apply that, as I pointed out the other day, for betterments and improvements, and for instalment payments upon equipment- principal payments on equipment. Having regard to the situation that exists at the present time-the liability incurred for interest, the payment on underlying securities, and the situation so far as concerns the next twelve months we will say-the rough estimate that I made after discussing the matter with the officials was that from $20,000,000 to $25,000,000 would be required. In other words, if we took the course we adopted last year, and made a round vote to the Canadian Northern of the sum required to meet liabilities and payments to be made in respect of interest upon securities in priority to the $45,000,000 mortgage of the Government, for betterments and for instalments upon rolling stock, about $20,000,000 to $25,000,000 would be required. With regard to short-term maturities which fall due over the next couple of years, I hope that the Canadian Northern officials will be able to renew those with the Government, the sole owner of the stock, just as they would expect to renew them if sixty per cent of the stock remained in the hands of private owners. I do not agree with the hon. member from Carleton (Mr. Carvell), and I will tell him why. After all, if money is seeking invest-

ment, it is a question of interest rate to be paid. These short-term loans of the Canadian Northern are pretty 'well secured. The loans in New York are secured with a substantial margin, upon bonds guaranteed by the Dominion Government and certain of the western provinces. That is very high-class collateral, and I expect the Canadian Northern officials will be able to renew the loans by Teason of the fact that the Government is the sole owner of the stock. What I have said is subject to this, that in these war times no man can tell what condition we may be in after one month or two, and it is possible that in one or more instances the Canadian Northern might not be -able to extend those loans. If they do not, then I think the Government, as sole owner-for it will be sole owner through its ownership of $100,000,000 of capital stock of the Canadian Northern- should protect its property. Assume we brought down a vote, as suggested by the hon. gentleman from 'Carleton, for $20,000,000 or $25,000,000, as we did last year, it is quite possible-although I do not apprehend it will take place-that during the year the Canadian Northern might not be able to renew one or more of those loans. Then you would have a difficult situation on your hands again. The real fact of the matter is that the essence of this Canadian Northern situation is that the Dominion Government, and the governments of nearly all the provinces of Canada, are so involved by their guarantees given during the years of the construction of this system that default cannot be allowed, and the Government, after giving the matter its most serious attention, and realizing all that my hon. friend from Carleton has put forward, reached the conclusion that if this system is not to be allowed to go into default, and if, in order to prevent default, the Government of Canada is obliged to put up $15,000,000 to $20,000,000 a year, and become practically sponsor for the financing of the system from year to year, we must take the next step and own that system for the people of Canada. The hon. gentleman from Carleton made a very interesting and very fair speech on this subject, and I asked him, when he suggested that we should take the course we took last year, what about next year? My hon. friend threw his mind ahead a year and considered the parliament of that time.
I think there is no doubt whatsoever that, war or no war, the Canadian Northern Railway would have to make application for assistance. I pointed out last year, in the -speech in which I introduced the esti-[*air Thomas White.]
mates for the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific, that the time had come when we should appoint a commission, with a view to reaching a final solution of this railway problem, the greatest problem in Canada, outside the war, without a doubt.
I stated also at that time that the solution might involve taking over one or more of the railway systems of Canada, and that there might be involved the possibility of the nationalization of all the railways of Canada. I pointed out to the House pretty fully the other day that the last was a very large order indeed, having regard to the fact that we are in the midst of a war and having regard also to the financial problems touched upon by certain gentlemen opposite. But, after giving the matter our best consideration we reached the conclusion that we should take this property for the people of Canada in order that, if we are to pay out huge sums of money year after year, the fruition of that expenditure should inure to the people of Canada, not to the private owners of the road. In other words, if we are to continue to finance this system, it must be owned by the people of Canada.
I do not know that it is necessary that I should refer to the remarks made by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German); I thought he had a very weak case when he had to resort to personal aspersions. This railway problem has been the most difficult problem with which any Government of Canada has been called upon to deal, outside of the war. Every year it presents itself, and it would continue to present itself. This year, after considering the whole situation and having regard to all the financial questions involved, we reached the conclusion that we should take this forward step, which is a step in the line indicated by the Drayton-Acworth report. To take over the whole of the railway systems would, I believe, be too serious a step for a Government to contemplate, having regard to the burden of the war. But by taking over the Canadian Northern and by lending assistance to the Grand Trunk Pacific-I pointed out that we could not deal with the Grand Trunk Pacific at this time as we are dealing with the Canadian Northern because most important negotiations would be involved with the Grand Trunk Railway company-it seemed to us that the proposals which I addressed to the House were the best under' all the circumstances, and I believe they are. I do not believe there

is any other solution of this . Canadian Northern railway problem that will meet the approval and support of public opinion in this country. I think that the Government have taken a proper step, and that looking to the future, we can see the working out of the recommendations of the majority report. No one can say at this stage how this railway, the Intercolonial, the National Transcontinental, and the Grand Trunk Pacific, if we should acquire it later, will be administered. It might be proper to administer them all by a board of experts constituted somewhat as suggested in the Drayton-Acworth report. I absolutely subscribe to the principle that if this system is to he efficiently administered it must be administered absolutely free from partisan interference.

I am glad to get that
admission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not an admission; that has been my principle throughout with regard to all these matters.

Does the minister feel
that it is possible to 'get the same results from mere officials that you can get from men who are vitally interested, as the owners and managers of a railroad are?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A good deal of weight is to be attached to the opinions put forward by my hon. friend; but the trend of public opinion is unmistakably along the line of these proposals. Nor is it a recent trend; it has gradually developed over a course of years. The whole tendency of public administration has been towards enlarging, not restricting, the functions of Government. I think we must look forward to that; I think we must have sufficient confidence in ourselves to believe that we can administer these enterprises; that we shall obtain officials who will manage them as efficiently as private enterprise will manage them. But even if we do not succeed in managing them quite as efficiently as private enterprise would manage them, still the advantages that will accrue to the public from public operation will more than counterbalance any defects in administration. This problem, as I say, has been here for years past-the problem of aiding these railways from time to time so that the systems may be completed and so that they may render service to the people. We believe that the time has come when we must discontinue affording this annual aid and [DOT]lay down the principle that if the Government is to do the financing the people must
have the benefit of the ownership of the system. I listened with much interest-I always do-to what the member for Carle-ton said, but I believe that this is the step called for by all the circumstances existing to-day, and the step that the people of this country demand, if these roads are to be maintained, as I think they should be, as solvent going concerns.
I do not intend to go over all the ground again; I shall refer briefly to the chief arguments advanced by the minister. He says that we have to put up money every year; I agree with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend said, over a period of five years; that is possibly correct.

I was arguing that, while you might get along with $15,000,000 or $20,000,000 a year, if you advanced money annually to the Canadian Northern railway system, the moment the Government attempted to operate the road they would put out $50,000,000 a year instead of $15,000,000. The Intercolonial is a Government enterprise; it goes through a good country; it is as badly operated as anything in the world could be, and we get no interest out of it. I believe the Minister of Railways does claim that he had a surplus of a million or two last year, but that was all by doing Government business; it was only a matter of bookkeeping. You get no interest on your investment, and you put out millions every year in order to keep the thing going. Sometimes I feel that I should like to know how much we are putting out on the Intercolonial railway every year; it would run into many millions. The same thing will happen if the Government take over the Canadian Northern railway system; we will put up millions-not $15,000,000, or $20,000,000 a year, but $50,000,000, $60,000,000, or $70,000,000. My hon. friend is correct when he says that there is a great trend of public opinion in Canada, especially in Ontario, in favour of public ownership. Public ownership of all sorts of utilities has been tried, but I have yet to see the public utility in Canada that in the matter of sound business management would compare for a moment with privately-owned and privately-operated utilities.
This afternoon I referred briefly to the Manitoba telephone system. The Manitoba Government took over the telephone business under very favourable circumstances. Does the minister know that to-day in no other place in Canada are the people pay-



ing such enormous prices for telephone service as the people of Manitoba are paying for a very indifferent service? They are, in many cases, paying from fifty to seventy-five per cent more for the service than the people in the Maritime Provinces are paying where the systems are privately owned and managed. Any public utility in Canada always costs more to operate under public ownership than it would if operated by a private enterprise. We are trying in this country to apply certain ideas and conditions that have been worked out fairly successfully in the Old Country. The bigger cities of Europe have operated tramway systems and other public utilities with a good deal of success; but for all that, we would not put up for two days with the service they have in those big cities.
Is my hon. friend sure about the tramways?

I am not sure, because I did not compare the tramways owned by the public with those owned by corporations. Take the telephone system in England. A man will wait half an hour to get telephone connection in England. He does not use the telephone; he uses the telegraph, simply because the telephone service is twenty years behind1 the times. The telegraph service is not any too good, but the telephone service is horrible. Yet we are told: Look at what the English people are doing; they are running the telephones in England. Yes, they are running them, but the people of this country would not put up with the service for two days.
My hon. friend speaks about the operation- of railroads. I have been on Government-owned railways in Germany, Holland and France and the first-class accommodation on many of the roads in Germany is not equal to what we call the tourist class in Canada. The people of Canada would not put up with the accommodation for a moment. If you are going to have public ownership of public utilities in Canada, and if you are going to get down to anything like the cost of operation by private corporations, you will have to make the service inferior, because in Canada you cannot operate a public utility for the same money as a private corporation can and give the same service. In my experience of travelling over a portion of the world, I do not think I have ever seen such an excellent service as the Canadian Pacific railway gives us. I go to New York very frequently; I travel along the northern part of the United States and there is no service there equal to that of the Canadian Pacific railway.
You ought to travel between Ottawa and Brockville. It takes four hours and fifteen minutes to go seventy-three miles.

There is no doubt that the Canadian Pacific is giving the finest service in the world to-day, and that is simply because the Canadian Pacific has been built up by men who have started at the bottom. Many of those men are alive to-day. It is unfortunate that many of them are passing .away. There is not a man at the top in the Canadian Pacific Railway company to-day who did not start at the bottom, and each one feels he has a real interest in the operation of the road; he feels he is a proprietor in some sense. There is a loyalty to the system that you cannot find on the Intercolonial, or any other Government-owned mad. I realize I am speaking to-night very much in opposition to current opinion in Canada. Nevertheless, those are my views, and I am stating them, no matter how they are received by the press and the people of Canada. Should my hon. friend happen to be Minister of Finance four or five years longer he will regret that he did not take the advice we are giving him this evening and not launch on this great principle of Government ownership of the Canadian Northern, which must inevitably carry along with it Government ownership of the Grand Trunk Pacific and possibly of the Grand Trunk as well.

In presenting certain information to the committee this afternoon, the Minister of Finance said that he thought he was bringing down all that had been asked for. Some hon. gentleman on this side-I think the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux)-asked the minister if he cpuld bring down the names of the shareholders and also the names of the directors.
The bondholders.
The names of the shareholders and directors were asked for.

To that list I would ask the minister to add the names of the pledgees of the stock to which he 'has referred and also the names of the contractors referred to in the printed statement as having unsettled claims. There are, in Ottawa and vicinity, some contractors who, to my knowledge, have unsettled claims, and if will be interesting to note if their names will appear on 'the list presented by the

minister or not. In that way we shall be able to judge as to the reliability of the statement .made iby the company. I should be glad to have that information from the minister before the Bill founded on the resolution is submitted to the House for discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be impossible for us to obtain the names of the bondholders of the Canadian Northern Railway company, as those bonds pass .from hand to hand and a holder to-day might not be a holder to-morrow. I do not think that matter would have any bearing upon the question before the committee, which is as to whether the Government shall acquire the entire capital stock of the Canadian Northern company. I will endeavour to get the other information asked for by my hon. friend. There is a further statement which I said I would lay upon the table of the House when the Bill is in the committee stage, when there will be ample time, to discuss all its provisions; that is the balance sheet for the fiscal year of the company which ended on June 30, 1917. I think I can get that substantially correct. Hon. members will understand that in a railway system as large as this, two or three months are required to check all the vouchers to a certain date. I will endeavour to get that statement. I think that is substantially all that has been asked for, but if when the Bill is in the committee stage, any further information is required, we could get it fairly expeditiously, without a delay of more than a day or so.
Will the minister get the information asked for before the Bill reaches the committee stage?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can get some. I might be able to get the balance sheet, although I hardly think so. I might be able to get the names of the shareholders. I will, at all events, endeavour to do so.

Suppose a constituent
of mine asks me: How much are you paying for the Canadian Northern? What shall I say to him?
Perhaps it is as well that you do not know.

An hon. member says: Perhaps it is as well that you do not know. I have been in a quandary as to. just what I would tell him. I know what the guaranteed liabilities are; I know what the unguaranteed liabilities are;
I know what the short-term liabilities are; but I do not know yet what it is going to cost us during the next three years for betterments, rolling stock, etc. That is what I had particularly in mind. There are certain works such as the Montreal tunnel and terminals, the terminals at Vancouver, and other works of a similar nature but of less importance. The Finance Minister, replying to a question with reference to the Montreal terminals, said that there was a certain amount of the $45,000,000 guaranteed bonds still with the Receiver General, and the proceeds were to be applied toward the completion of the Montreal terminals. How much remains in the Receiver General's hands, and is it sufficient to complete the terminals at Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told so.

I should also like to have the same information regarding the Vancouver terminals, and other improvements of a smaller nature. These will come under the immediate liabilities, if liabilities they are.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will ask the Financial Comptroller of the Railway Department to have a statement prepared showing the financing in connection with the Montreal tunnel and the Vancouver terminals. My recollection is that an issue of bonds was made by the Montreal Terminal and Tunnel company. These bonds were sold in New York and the proceeds applied to the construction of the tunnel and the terminals. The amount required to complete the work is available, I am informed by the Railway Department, from the proceeds of the $45,000,000 of bonds guaranteed by the Dominion Government remaining in the hands of the Receiver General. The same statement is made respecting the Vancouver terminals. But I will obtain that information specifically and give it to the House when the Bill is in committee.
There was one point I inadvertently overlooked in answering my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy) and that was with reference to the item of $1,300,000 due to contractors. I am told by the Financial Comptroller of the Railway Department that ' practically all the contractors' accounts, with the exception of about $100,000, have been completely cleared up, and that this $1,300,000 represents principally drawbacks against construction. While there may be some contested claims outside, I do not think that they are of any considerable consequence. But I shall endeavour to obtain that information so that when we are

considering the Bill in committee it will be available to hon. gentlemen.
I understand that some claims have been made within the week.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the claims are against Mackenzie and Mann, our taking over of the stock of the Canadian Northern would have no immediate bearing on that, except that those claims could no doubt be settled out of the award to be made by the arbitrators in respect of the value of the shares, if they are not settled in the meantime. However, that aspect of the matter does not immediately concern the proposal before the committee.

The difficulty is this- and I urged it before: The ordinary contractor will not differentiate between the Canadian Northern and Mackenzie and Mann. He will say: The Government has taken over a mile of road that I have built, and I have not got my money; and I want it. The Government will have to make provision to meet those cases.

I shall reserve what I have to say on this matter until the Bill comes before the House, but whether the Bill comes up now or later, I wish once more to register my protest against this legislation. I believe that it should not have been brought up during the present session; indeed, it should not have been brought up during the war. The Government creates the impression throughout the country that we have money to burn. According to rumour, and, indeed, according to legislation passed since 1911, this Government might well be defined as being the creation of the Canadian Northern, and it looks as if it would end with the Canadian Northern. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance, who is versed in the classics, should remember that famous apostrophe of Mirabeau during the French Revolution. Addressing himself to his colleagues in the Assembly, at the time the Minister of Finance was proposing that Frenchmen should contribute one-quarter of their revenues to maintain and save the State, he said: "Messieurs, la banqueroute est a vos portes et vous de'liberez," or, "Gentlemen, bankruptcy is staring you in the face, and yet you are discussing." I think it is well to remind the Minister of Finance this evening of those words of Mirabeau, because if bankruptcy is not staring us in the face, we are living in most crucial times at all events, and yet we are discussing whether or not we shall make another gift of several million dollars to 
Mackenzie and Mann. From the day he became Finance Minister, my hon. friend has thought of nothing else but giving slices of Canada's fortune to those two gentlemen.
Last session $15,000,000 was given to them. In 1914 their bonds were guaranteed to the amount of $45,000,000, and the Government took a share in the company, promising the country that this would he the last call on the public treasury, and that it would save the situation. This year we are to take over the company and control the whole $100,000,000 of stock. Last year my hon. friend appointed a commission of three most distinguished gentlemen-Mr. Acworth, an authority on railways in England, and, indeed, in Europe; Mr. Smith, one of the best railway men in America; and the Chairman of our own Railway Commission, Sir Henry Drayton. They prepared a report which has been published throughout the country, and which states in the most emphatic manner that the stock of the Canadian Northern company is valueless, and that Mackenzie and Mann are not entitled to any equity. And yet my hon. friend comes before Parliament in the dying days of this session, on the eve of a general election, with a proposition that Canada shall acquire the whole system by getting control of the stock. But whilst we assume all the liabilities he proposes to leave the management to the same individuals. He has the temerity to propose to the Canadian Parliament that the value of the stock shall be determined by arbitration. One arbitrator will be appointed by the Government, another by Mackenzie and Mann, and those two appointees will *appoint a third. I am not so gullible as to believe that these three arbitrators will not be friends of the company; everybody knows that they will he. Mackenzie and Mann will appoint a friend of their own; the Government, which is the creation of Mackenzie and Mann, will appoint a friend of Mackenzie and Mann, and the two together will appoint a third friend of Mackenzie and Mann. In this way a combination will be formed to fleece the country of several million dollars. My hon. friend must not forget that he stated not long ago that the public debt of this country amounted in round figures to one billion dollars; that we shall owe at the end of this war nearer two billion dollars than one and a half billion dollars; that we are spending every day towards our military effort about $800,000; that we are borrowing today at six per cent, selling our bonds at 98.

Yesterday, the Prime 'Minister chided me because I dared speak of economy on the appointment of a new minister overseas, and two under-secretaries. He said that my advocacy of economy should not be taken too seriously. Sir, if the Canadian Northern had not chloroformed the press of this country, my hon. friend would know what is the sentiment of the .people from one end of Canada to the other, and he would realize what the people think of this transaction which in my humble judgment is nothing less than a scandalous transaction. Not to speak of economy! When the revenues of every man, woman and child of this country -are being taxed in order to replenish the Treasury of Canada so that we may meet the contingencies of the war. My hon. friend has read Gladstone, the greatest Chancellor of the Exchequer England ever had. I read in one of his speeches many years ago the following words:	" A Chancellor of the Exchequer who is not ready to be cheese-paring is not worth his salt." Does my hon. friend realize the situation to-day? Does he not know that every man and woman in this country is working and saving in order that we ,may pass successfully through the present awful crisis? We have not saved one penny on the ordinary expenditures of the country. I say to my hon. friend that we had a right to expect from him in 1914 that in view of the waT he would reduce the ordinary expenditure by at least twenty-five or thirty per cent. He has not done so; on the contrary, he has increased it. At the end of the session last year my hon. friend came with another scandalous proposition-the Quebec and Saguenay deal. The scheme involved several million dollars, and was referred to the Exchequer Court. Sir Walter Cassels declared in his judgment that at least three-quarters of the claim made by the owners of the Quebec and Saguenay railway should not be paid by the Government. If this transaction goes through, the least my hon. friend should do would be to discard the idea of an arbitration which admittedly will go in favour of Mackenzie and Mann, and refer the whole question as to the value of the stock to Sir Walter Cassels, a man eminently fit to preside over .such a transaction, and in whom the .people of this country have every confidence. I am sincere when I register my protest against this resolution, and I say again, if the press of Canada had not been chloroformed by the Canadian Northern, there would not be room enough in. this building to hold all
the protests and all the petitions which would be made against this scandalous deal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) has been the first to introduce a political bias into the consideration of this question. He has waxed quite rhetorical over the fact that during the last four or five years the Government has had to deal with the Canadian Northern Railway situation. I would like to ask my hon. friend what he had to say during the years when the foundation was laid, so far as the Canadian Northern Railway company, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company, and the National Transcontinental Railway company are concerned, for all the difficulties- which have confronted this Government since 1911. Does my hon. friend think this Government went out looking for those railway problems? Those problems were here when we came into office. They have been with us every year, insistent, and urgent. They could not be evaded by the Government, if it had any regard to the credit, of this country, or of its provinces, or to financial conditions, or to the public service rendered by the transportation companies of Canada. What is the essence of the railway situation to-day?' # It is that we have three transcontinental railway systems where we ought to have two. I am not desirous to-night of carrying on a controversial discussion, but it has been started by my hon. friend from Rouville, and I must say something in defence of the Government with respect to the charges my hon. friend has made against it. We found the National Transcontinental unfinished. The Transcontinental from Moncton to Winnipeg which was to have cost $60,000,000 according to the estimate of the then Finance Minister, stands Canada to-day at $200,000,000. Does my hon. friend say this Government is responsible for that expenditure? Who is responsible for the $200,000,000 expended on the National Transcontinental? Take the Grand Trunk difficulties, referred to in the Drayton-Ac-worth report. Who is responsible for the bargain which brought about the situation by which the Grand Trunk is liable as guarantor to the extent of $5,000,000 annually on the securities issued by the Grand Trunk Pacific? Is this Government responsible for it? This Government cannot be responsible, because that bargain was entered into in 1904, -many years before the present. Government came into power. We had to provide money for the completion of the National Transcontinental. We had to make loans to the Grand Trunk Pacific if it was

to be completed. Although the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Canadian Northern as well, were enterprises originated by the Government of my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) when in power, I have always dealt fairly, as Minister of Finance, and this Government has always . dealt fairly with the Grand Trunk Pacific. We finished the National Transcontinental. The money was found, and the work was completed.
It is not completed yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is in process of completion. I suppose, as my hon. friend is aware, it may be said that railways are always in process of completion. My hon. friend knows that immediately after coming into power we made a loan of $16,000,000 to the Grand Trunk Pacific. We made another loan, of $8,000,000 to the Grand Trunk Pacific last yeaT. This year we have brought down an estimate of $7,500,000 for the same company. We did not do that because we want to do it, in the *sense of desiring to spend the money; we did it because the situation calls for financial aid if those roads are to continue to be operated. We have not gone out looking for an opportunity to spend money for the National Transcontinental or the Grand Trunk Pacific.
What I have said also applies to the Canadian Northern. When we came into power we found the road partially completed between Montreal and Port Arthur, with a guarantee of $35,000,000 upon it given by the late Government. This was not nearly sufficient to finish the line, and the Government found itself in the position in 1914. just as we find ourselves in the position today, of having to extend further aid to the Canadian Northern company ot allow the whole system to go into default, with great loss of money in connection with the guarantees given by the Dominion. I need not refer to the extensive aid by way of guarantee given to the Canadian Northern Railway system in the West. That is well known to the House, because it has been so frequently discussed here. The point I desire to make is that this Government found a certain railway situation when it came into power; that that railway situation has developed, has gone en to its inevitable conclusion in the completion of those lines, and that the Government of Canada has been meeting that situation as best it could from year to year. As I say, I am not disposed at this time to be critical of my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in regard to his Grand Trunk Pacific project. This is not a good time to be con-

troversial. We all realize that the times are serious. I have refrained from introducing any partisan or controversial matter into this debate because I think the attention of the House and of the country should be fixed, so far as possible, on our prosecution of the war, because that is the principle business of the time. But we are confronted with a condition and not a theory. If it was a theory we should not have to bring down these proposals. But it is a condition, a condition arising out of what was done by this Parliament and. by the legislative assemblies of the provinces of Canada years ago. We are confronted with a condition which has been fully disclosed in this House, and it has been common ground on both sides of the House-my hon. friend's leader, the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has taken the position again and again-that these roads must not be allowed to go into receiverships. If they are not to go into the hands of a receiver, they must be saved, and the only way to save them, so far as I know, is to continue to finance them. My hon. friend speaks of arbitration; he condemns the Government for the proposal that these shares should be valued by arbitration. Let me tell him that he voted for that in 1914.
I would refer the whole matter to Sir Walter Cassels.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend voted in 1914 for valuation by arbitration on an amendment moved by his leader, the right hon. leader of the Opposition. My hon. friend cannot deny that.
But we had not a debt of a billion and a half dollars then, and we were not at war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend can sing high and can sing low, and can blow hot and cold. It would not make any difference-he would be opposed to any proposal that this Government brought down in connection with this railway matter, for which we are not primarily responsible at all. My hon. friend would object. If we had brought down a proposal that this should be referred to the court, my hon. friend would have fallen back on his position, of 1914 and said that the value should be determined by arbitration; he would say it would take two years to determine this in the courts, and that in the meantime the matter would be hung up indefinitely, and he would have all kinds of suspicions against the Government. That is what my hon. friend would do because, while he is a good fellow per-

sonally, he cannot help being a violent and truculent partisan in the House.
What about yourself?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is impossible for me to be a partisan that is a matter of temperament. My hon. friend from Pic-tou (Mr. Macdonald) has a great advantage over me in that respect, because he was born a partisan.
I admit it frankly, you don't. You are not frank.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a great help -to my hon. friend. It is a great help to a man to be born with a bias.
Like you have, but you do not admit it.
Some men are born with it, and some acquire it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not arguing in a controversial manner. I think that both sides of this House,at this critical time, should take into consideration the conditions which surround this railway problem, the most important, next to the war, that we have, and discuss it in a businesslike manner, eliminating partisanship and political controversy altogether. It is too big a problem to be mixed up with the political situation-altogether too big a problem.
I have given all the reasons that moved the Government to take the course we have taken, and notwithstanding the strictures of the hon. member for Rouville I believe it is the course which will best meet the railway situation and will be a step forward in the policy of preserving for the people what the people have financed; and I believe that it is supported by public opinion throughout this country. I do not agree with my hon. friend for one moment that the press otf this country has been chloroformed. On the contrary, the policy which we have .adopted is a policy which has been advocated by the great majority of the press throughout Canada, not only recently, but for a considerable time past. The press of this country are a great public influence, and, so far as I have been able to judge, on the whole a great influence for good, and for progressive government. My hon. friend from Rouville might do a good deal worse than follow the judgment of the press. I do not know .any better way of forming the judgment of a public man than for him to study assiduously
the editorial expressions of the press. They are good public men who are in charge of newspapers in Canada, and they know the trend of public opinion. My hon. friend is entirely wrong in casting reflections upon the press of the country. There has been a widespread expression of opinion since these proposals have been brought down, and they have met with general .acceptance.
I may say to the hon. member for Rouville that in Ontario, from which province I come, these proposals are received .as embodying the proper policy to be pursued by the Government of Canada in connection with this most difficult question. I say to my hon. friend that he would make no headway in Ontario-il do not believe he would make any headway in the West-
Not with your arbitration attached to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-in attacking the policy of public ownership which the Government has introduced. In answer to my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German),
I would repeat what has been said many times to-day, that in determining upon arbitration we are following the method which was suggested by the Drayton-Acworth report .as to the number of shares which might be allowed to remain with the present owners and as to the earnings which .might be attributable to those shares.
You are not doing that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: times-the water has gone over the wheel, the wheat is out of the straw; it is waste of time for this House, at this of all times, to discuss the question of the, railway policy. We have three transcontinental railway systems in Canada; no matter what we may say about the past, they are here; they have their requirements; the situation must be met, and it is for the Government of the day to determine what is the best policy to be adopted in order to meet it. These proposals which we have brought down represent the policy which we think right, and which we regard as in the public interest at this time, and I believe they will met with the general approval of the people.

My hon. friend said he did not wish to discuss the water that has gone through the mill, but he did it just the same. The matter under consideration is the Canadian Northern, and I will confine my remarks to that concern. The hon. gentleman knows I am not averse at any time to discuss the other matter, but this is what we have in mind, and I will just refer to it for a moment. If the policy of the late Government, with which I had something to do, had been carried out, we should not have been found in the position we are to-day in reference to the Canadian Northern system. I do not say for a moment that that system would not have had its difficulties, and that we should not have had to come, in a measure, to its relief, possibly owing to financial stringency and unforeseen conditions. But the policy of the late Government in connection with the Canadian Northern was this: to first connect its gathering system in the West with the Atlantic system, before it ventured across the Rockies. Aid was given to that system to reach its coal mines, but the late Government refused absolutely to give aid to the Canadian Northern system west of the Rocky mountains for the time being. Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann then went to the British Columbia Government, and made an arrangement with the late Sir Richard McBride, building the British Columbia end of this road under a provincial, not a federal, charter. They came again to the Dominion Government, and were again refused any aid, for the time being at least, for that portion of the transcontinental line. They entered into an agreement with the late Sir Richard McBride, by which he aided them very liberally, as we find by this statement laid on the table of the House-$40,000,000 I

think. In connection with that aid Mackenzie and Mann entered into a signed agreement with Sir Richard McBride that that portion of their transcontinental line should not come under the jurisdiction of the Dominion Board of Railway Commissioners. So extreme was that arrangement that Mackenzie and Mann agreed that if any person attempted to bring that portion, even as to through rates, before the Board of Railway Commissioners, they would appear personally and oppose the application. Now, this Government, coming into power, reversed that policy altogether, and they came to the aid of the Canadian Northern railway west of the Rocky Mountains. I submit that if the Canadian 'Northern railway had strictly adhered to the plan of first connecting up its gathering system on the prairies' with the Atlantic seaboard, and got that system into operation before they attempted to build the British Columbia end of the line, they would not have been in the serious condition we find them in to-day.
I asked the Finance Minister a question, and he said he was going to answer, but we got away into something else. I said, suppose one of my constituents were to ask what is the Canadian Northern system going to cost us, what should I tell him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As to stock?
No, everything.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All that we are buying is the stock.
We do not know what we are going to pay for that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, because we do not know its value. It may be little or it may be more. It will be for the Board of Arbitrators to determine that. I stated yesterday that I would not be frank if I did not say to the House that the Government, after acquiring the stock of the system, intended to continue it as a going concern, and while we are not legally liable for the debts of the company, any more than my hon. friend would be liable for the debts of the Canadian Pacific railway if he happened to buy some of the shares, at the same time the Government intends it should continue as a going concern, and, of course, would from time to time render such assistance as might be necessary to that end. The hon. membeT from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) made some pretty shrewd observations to-night, among them the statement that he thought the Canadian North-

ern in a period of five years would fie selfsupporting. I find a considerable opinion among those competent to judge that this Canadian Northern Railway system is likely in time to be a decidedly paying concern.
It depends on the management.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, it depends largely on the management, and, of course, upon conditions, but there seems to be no doubt that the Government is taking over a good railway system. It is well located, with excellent grades, and with alignment that leaves nothing to be desired. I feel quite optimistic with regard to the future of the Canadian Northern Railway system, once it gets over this trying period referred to by the hon. member from Carleton. My hon. friend (Mr. Graham) says his constituents might ask him, what liabilities will the Government have to assume? I think he might reply something like this:	In
the stock ownership of a Tailway system is embraced the physical properties, the plant and equipment of the system. Those are assets which every year produce a certain amount of earnings. So far as the Canadian Northern is concerned, those earnings will probably in time be able to take care of underlying interest charges, betterments and improvements, and possibly purchases of a certain amount of rolling stock. Supposing that situation is reached, we have a great property that produces every year sufficient revenue to take care of the operating expenses, the fixed charges and the other matters I have mentioned. Therefore, the question of liability need not at that time particularly disturb the people of Canada any more than the liabilities of the Canadian Pacific railway to-day disturb its shareholders. The Canadian Pacific railway has liabilities, -but the earning power of the company is so great that no shareholder is in the least degree disturbed as to these liabilities, because the earning power is ample to take care of the interest upon all the bonded debt, and also pay handsome dividends to the shareholders. So far as the immediate situation is concerned, I have told the House that on account of the Canadian Northern being unable, owing -to war conditions and to the position of its securities, to do new financing-as a railway company in a better position would be able to do, at least in peace time-to provide for betterment, for rolling stock and for expenditures of the capital nature, the Dominion Government might have to provide fifteen or
tiventy million dollars every year, for the next three or four or even five years, as my hon. friend from Carleton has stated, in order to meet underlying interest charges and to assist the company in its financing. But this situation differs from the situation which has hitherto prevailed, and which would continue to prevail if the Government brought down a Bill to aid the Canadian Northern by way of loan, as it did last year. All the expenditures which we shall make from this forward will be for the benefit of the property which is owned and controlled by the people of Canada.
That is the essential difference between the situation now and the situation that existed hitherto. With regard to the value of the shares themselves, my hon-. friend may tell his constituents that he approves of the manner of ascertaining the value, because the course adopted was the course re-commended by the leader of the Opposition. As soon as he tells his loyal constituents that the right hon. leader of the Opposition recommended that course in 1914, I am positive that they will be quite satisfied and will vote for him as usual.
The name of the leader of the Opposition is the best name in my constituency, by all odds.

Just like the West.
-Mr. GRAHAM:	But the people might
change their views, as my hon. friend did, for instance, in certain matters- connected with the conscription measure. I am afraid that I shall have to make up an answer myself for my constituents, because they will not understand the one given by the Finance Minister.

Is it intended that the operation of the road under the auspices of the Government will begin when the transfer of the stock is -made, or will it be postponed until aftpr the val-ue has been fixed by -the arbitrators and the -amount has been actually paid over?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under the terms of the agreement, as soon as the five-sixths of the stock is vested in the minister, the Government will be in a position to aid the Canadian Northern in connection with its financing and to control the board.
Will the Government at that time make -any changes in the board that will interfere with the present method of operation by the directors now in control?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is premature to make any statement in advance of con-

sideration of the question by the Government when it becomes the owner of the shares. But the Government will have to consider the personnel of the Board of Directors of the Canadian Northern and determine what, if any, changes should be made. I mean that the Government will then be in a position to determine the personnel. I pointed out the other day that the road is well managed. So far as the operating officials are concerned many of them are of the highest standing; I mentioned two or three of them by name. It is not in mind that any changes will take place. The Government's function will be to appoint a Board of Directors to administer through the officials the affairs of the road. The Government will not be brought into immediate privity with the officials of the road; in other words, the Government will be the sole stockholder of the road and as such will be entitled to name the board of directors. The directors will have general supervision over the affairs of the company just as the directors have now.

The Government will be the owners of the stock and in that respect there will be Government ownership of the road, but there will not be Government operation. That would seem to be the purpose. My hon. friend lauded the desirability of Government ownership of railways. That phrase "Government ownership of railways" is very broad in its acceptation. It may mean that the Government simply have title to a railway and that somebody else is operating it, or it may mean that the Government owns and operates the utility. In this case we are having Government ownership in the former sense, not in the latter. My hon. friend since he became Finance Minister, has frequently come to Parliament in regard to the matter of aid to the Canadian Northern. We - remember that in the early stage of his career he came to us and wanted us to vote $15,000,000 for that purpose. On that occasion he gave the House the impression that if we voted $15,000,000, that ' would be the last time of asking; that ithe Canadian Northern Railway company would be able to handle everything in connection with their affairs and that the country would not have any further trouble in the matter. We had a homily to-night from my hon. friend with regard to some views expressed by the member for Rou-ville (Mr. Lemieux). My hon. friend forgets that he supported my right hon. leader in 1904 in his project of assisting in the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific rail-
way and that he remained a supporter of that proposal right down to 1911. Certainly my hon. friend cannot deny that he is a political acrobat-I do not know whether that is worse than being a partisan or not. My hon. friend exercised his acrobatic propensities in 1911 in respect of the matter of trade between Canada and the country to the south of us. Only quite recently, after denouncing free wheat and all such things as matters emanating from the Evil One, my hon. friend, with the greatest possible ease and eloquence, dilated upon the glorious advantage of having free wheat and freedom of trade north and south. I have said that when he asked us for the $15,000,000 for the Canadian Northern, we were told that that was the last time of asking. When he asked for $45,000,000 the proposal was opposed on this side of the House, an amendment being moved for a six months' hoist and issue being taken in the matter as between the parties. My hon. friend said that the country should congratulate itself upon the fact that it had obtained forty per cent of the stock and had made a good bargain. All that my hon. friend said in 1914 when he proposed the advancing of $45,000,000 will be called up in evidence against him before this board of arbitration which he proposes to appoint to fix the value of the stock. All his statements will be available for the counsel of the Canadian Northern people when they go before this board of arbitration. They will argue that if my hon. friend could buy $40,000,000 of stock for $45,000,000, the old rule of proportion would enable the board to ascertain what $60,000,000 of stock was worth. They can make a very fair argument to any tribunal based upon my hon. friend's attitude at that time. My hon. friend is now trying to ride the Government ownership horse, and in order that he may do so he is assuming a debt for this country in the vicinity of $600,000,000. My hon. friend is taking a very large order. He had the temerity the other day, on August 1, when the member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) intimated that the country was assuming a liability of $500,000,000 to say:
That is entirely incorrect. The corporate entity of the Canadian Northern railway and of all the companies in the system is being preserved, and we are going to operate through the Canadian Northern Railway company. It is not even an indirect liability.
